episode_thesis: Git argues the March 2026 Iran-war shock was a risk-off event (stocks and bonds sold off together, oil spiked at the front of the curve only) and that CTAs should hedge a common first factor (duration) instead of scaling every position when spreads widen. A flow-based excess-volatility paper (value, noise and trend traders) is reviewed and critiqued, and CTA market-universe breadth is framed by correlation and capacity.

speakers.role: Systematic fixed-income researcher/trader and co-host of the Systematic Investor series; works with Tom Babbage on commodities
speakers.speaker_note: Caption labels the name Yuval/Yoav; ledger uses Yoav Git. Fixed income is his area; commodity view is relayed from colleague Tom Babbage.

worldview_premises.premise: Inflation regimes make the stock-bond correlation positive, so bonds fail as an equity hedge.
worldview_premises.support: March 2026 selloffs in both; earlier talks

worldview_premises.premise: Western fiscal stress makes inflation a way to erode debt, so higher yields are near-inevitable but untimeable.
Back-of-curve oil reflects fundamental supply and demand and is insulated from news-cycle shocks ('weather vs climate').
Most volatility is noise; the EMH holds either because price is right (Shiller) or because there is no true price.
Markets are populated by three flows: value traders revert to target, noise traders inject volatility, trend followers trade returns.
Genuine jumps in fundamental value (payrolls, weekend war) move prices without trading.
worldview_premises.support: Examples: payroll liquidity shrinks then gaps, weekend Iran attack

worldview_premises.premise: Value traders also face risk limits, so an unbounded (cubic) response is unrealistic.
Capacity limits risk per market so footprint remains unwindable; more AUM pushes risk into the biggest markets.
CTA return is diversification times average market Sharpe; the value of many markets depends on their correlation.

decision_process.practice: Scale each market down in stress by volatility (standard CTA); alternative: hedge the common first factor while limiting specific risk per market.
Time of day of execution matters in a $20-25 oil daily range, making tracking of one's own model hard.
Scenario analysis back to 1998 for surprise volatility: March 2026 ranked at the top.
Estimate noise, value and trend populations with the EM algorithm (unlabelled mixtures).
Choose market universe by correlation and capacity: correlated big markets for index-like CTA; low-correlation markets need capacity thinking.
Limit risk per market so the footprint can be unwound in a crisis.

speakers.evidence_style: First-hand trading experience of March 2026, literature review of a flow-model paper, and simple economic reasoning; scenario analysis on history.

current_views.view: March 2026 was a risk-off event, not just inflation: bonds sold off as much as equities and gold fell.
current_views.reasoning: Long-end sell-off, EM back of curve

current_views.view: Higher yields are near-inevitable (fiscal stress, 2-year auction weakness) but timing unknowable.
Fixed-income trend trading has been difficult since 2023: moves reverse violently within the month.
Oil: front-end spike due to supply constraints; the long end structurally oversupplied.
The flow-model paper's calibration (noise first order, value second, trend negligible) matches the view that CTA footprints are small.
Critique of the paper: ignores genuine jumps, cubic value response, monthly data, no predictive use.

worldview_premises.premise: Narratives are unpredictable (Danish election, gold in the Iran war), which supports a rules-based approach.
Short-window dispersion between CTAs is largely initial-positioning luck, not model quality.
CTAs only lose less than bonds in surprises; they cannot claim protection.
Core-market CTAs can cut duration cheaply in stress; alternative-market CTAs face higher costs, hidden in monthly performance.
Keeping illiquid positions hedged with futures is dangerous in a liquidity crisis (correlations go to one, exits close).
In practice replicators have modest correlation to the CTA index and substantial tracking error.

positions.speaker: Yoav Git
positions.position: Scaling every position is expensive in alternative markets (closing a long-short book could cost on the order of 5%); a factor hedge via Treasury futures is better.

positions.position: For core-market CTAs this is cheap; the problem is specific to alternative markets and is hidden in monthly returns.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The 5% cost of closing a long-short alternative book is illustrative ('let's say'), not measured.
Git 'does not have the model' for the factor-hedge idea; no test shown.
Flow sequence in March (CTA, value close-out, real money, squeeze) is narrated without flow data.

Paper's calibration result (trend negligible) sits oddly with Git's remark that CTAs feature prominently in such models; the reader must reconcile prominence in the model structure with negligible estimated contribution.
Back-of-curve oil is insulated 'weather vs climate' is attributed to a colleague and not evidenced.
Unverified: private credit gating, apparent pre-announcement trading in oil.

forward_looking_inputs: Observable inputs: spreads and liquidity costs in EM rates, front vs back of oil curve, stock-bond correlation, auction demand, CTA flows after volatility gaps, value-trader stop-outs. Horizon: weeks for flows, years for fiscal-driven yield rise.
reader_inferences: The flow model attributes first-order volatility to noise and negligible footprint to trend followers, which means trend following cannot be justified as a major source of price formation by this paper; the paper uses monthly data so cannot settle daily dynamics.
Git's proposal is a risk-management rule change (factor-based de-risking) rather than a forecast.
